stories.who: China's ruling Communist Party and its cabinet, the State Council, in policy guidelines issued on Friday, as cited by the state news agency Xinhua
stories.what: told officials to avoid blind investment and 'swarm-like' rushes into high-tech sectors while still pushing A I research, computing power and pilot bases; officials whose blind investment causes major losses will be held to account; the guidelines set direction and do not yet show how that will be enforced
stories.why_for_people: Beijing wants China's A I boom not to turn into a costly bubble of wasteful overbuilding, which touches Chinese investors and A I firms, though the guidelines set direction only
stories.script: From Beijing. China's ruling party and cabinet told officials to avoid blind rushes into high tech, so the A I boom does not become a costly bubble.
stories.screen: photorealistic news footage: a slow aerial shot over a brand-new high-tech industrial park on the edge of a Chinese city, rows of identical glass office towers and half-finished server halls with cranes still on them, wide empty boulevards between them, grey smog light, no people, no signs, no readable text

stories.who: TypeSafe A I, a Californian start-up backed by the venture firms Andreessen Horowitz, Sequoia and DCVC
stories.what: raised eight hundred and seventy million dollars at a seven and a half billion dollar value, weeks after releasing Jev, an A I that does not write text but gives probabilities it calls calibrated decisions; the company claims a third of the biggest U S firms already use it, a claim not independently checked
stories.why_for_people: big money is backing an A I that gives odds instead of words, so firms may let machines make more of their choices, though the adoption figure is the company's own claim
stories.script: In finance. A I start-up TypeSafe raised nearly nine hundred million dollars for an A I that gives odds instead of words, so firms may let machines choose.
stories.screen: photorealistic news footage: the glass front of a Silicon Valley start-up office at dusk, then inside a bright trading-style floor where staff seen from behind watch a large wall display of green and red probability bars rising and falling, no readable words, numbers or logos

stories.who: leaders at OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, at an-thropic, maker of the Claude chatbot, and at other A I companies, according to unnamed insiders quoted by one outlet
stories.what: are reportedly rehearsing in private how to handle the public and political backlash after a catastrophic A I event, with a large cyberattack that shuts down banking, internet, power or water the scenario they fear most; plans reportedly include stress-testing defences and briefing members of Congress; OpenAI says its preparedness exercises are not treated as inevitable and an-thropic declined to comment
stories.why_for_people: the companies building A I reportedly expect a major A I disaster within a year and are already planning for the backlash, which would touch everyone if banks or power were hit; the account rests on unnamed insiders
stories.script: Next, safety. A I firms OpenAI and an-thropic reportedly plan for the backlash to an A I disaster that insiders expect within a year.
stories.screen: photorealistic news footage: a bank branch's row of cash machines at night with every screen gone black and a queue of people seen from behind, then a city skyline where whole blocks of windows go dark one after another, no readable words or logos

stories.who: Feather Robotics, a start-up in East Palo Alto, California, led by chief executive and co-founder Hoa Mai
stories.what: launched a two-armed humanoid robot on a wheeled base priced under thirty thousand dollars, sold as a body only, so customers run A I from developers such as Nvidia, Skild or Physical Intelligence on it; by the company's figures each arm carries four pounds, fifteen at peak, it fits through standard doors and its swappable batteries last ten hours; no independent test
stories.why_for_people: a humanoid robot that carries light loads is now cheap enough that small teams could afford one instead of building hardware, though every figure is the company's own
stories.script: In robotics. U S start-up Feather Robotics launched a wheeled humanoid that carries light loads for under thirty thousand dollars, so small teams could afford one.
stories.screen: photorealistic news footage: a white humanoid robot with two arms on a round wheeled base glides through a standard office doorway in a small start-up workshop, picks a cardboard box off a bench with both hands and sets it on a shelf, a touch screen on its chest showing only a plain blue glow, no readable words or logos

stories.who: Elon Musk, chief executive of the rocket and A I company SpaceXAI, replying to an-thropic, the A I company behind the Claude chatbot, and its new rule
stories.what: replied 'I think this is the right move' (Gizmodo reports) to a post about an-thropic's new usage policy, which bans sustained and needless cruelty toward its Claude A I models from the twelfth of November; an-thropic says it applies only to extreme cases with no purpose, not frustration, pushback, dark creative themes or testing, and has not said exactly what counts as abuse; we carried the policy as a short item in our ninth of October edition, so this is a follow-up to yesterday's story
stories.why_for_people: a top tech leader backs the rule we reported yesterday that bars Claude users from needless cruelty to the A I from November, though an-thropic has not said what counts as cruel
stories.script: On chatbots. SpaceXAI chief executive Elon Musk replied that an-thropic's ban on needless cruelty to its Claude A I we reported yesterday is the right move.
stories.screen: photorealistic news footage: over the shoulder of a person at a kitchen table at night, hands hammering a laptop keyboard, the chatbot window on the screen with blurred unreadable lines, then the conversation panel closing to a blank pale screen and the hands stopping, no readable words or logos, no face

stories.who: Ting-Wei Sun, a contractor who worked with the U S server maker Super Micro Computer; Super Micro itself has not commented
stories.what: pleaded guilty on Thursday in a Manhattan federal court to a plot to ship servers holding advanced Nvidia A I chips to China against U S export rules, routed through a Southeast Asian company that hid the Chinese buyers; prosecutors say the plot covered about two and a half billion dollars of A I technology; the charges against two other men, one a Super Micro co-founder, are still allegations
stories.why_for_people: the U S rules meant to keep its best A I chips away from China are being broken and enforced: a guilty plea shows how top chips were smuggled to Chinese buyers
stories.script: In court. A contractor for server maker Super Micro admitted smuggling N-vidia A I chips to Chinese buyers, breaking U S rules that keep top chips from China.
stories.screen: photorealistic news footage: the stone steps and columns of the Manhattan federal courthouse on a grey morning with a few figures in dark coats seen from behind, then a dim warehouse where gloved hands lift a black rack-mounted A I server into a wooden shipping crate marked only with plain tape, no logos or readable words

stories.who: Nikon, the Japanese camera maker that runs the Small World In Motion microscope video contest; the disqualified winner is Dr Ning Xu of Tsinghua University in China
stories.what: disqualified the winning video, which showed hair-like cilia moving in the airway of a child with the lung disease PCD, after scientists such as Dr Robert Hirst of the University of Leicester said the cells looked nothing like real ones; Nikon ruled that generative A I was used in composing it against the contest rules, Xu says he believed he was within the rules, and Nikon will review the rules
stories.why_for_people: A I can fake even scientific footage, but experts spotted that the cells looked fake and Nikon stripped the prize, so the checks on A I-made science images are being tested in public
stories.script: In science. Camera maker Nikon stripped a Chinese scientist of its microscope prize for using A I, after experts said the cells in his video looked fake.
stories.screen: photorealistic news footage: a research microscope in a university lab with a scientist's gloved hands at the focus wheel, and on the monitor beside it a magnified blue-tinted field of cells with tiny hair-like strands beating in a wave, then the image freezing and a hand lifting a small framed award off a shelf, no readable words or logos, no face

fun.who: Pavel Rabtsevich, a twenty-eight-year-old product manager in Spain with no formal astronomy training
fun.what: used the A I coding tools Claude Code and Codex to search public data from NASA's TESS space telescope and found a star about a hundred and sixteen light-years away whose light dips every three days, a pattern that could mean a planet about one point four times Earth's size; NASA's TESS will watch the star from the end of October to test his predictions, and a NASA scientist says the hard part is ruling out false alarms such as twin stars
fun.why_for_people: with A I tools an untrained amateur can now spot a possible planet in public space data, though NASA must still check it next month and it may turn out to be a false alarm
fun.script: On a lighter note. A product manager in Spain with no astronomy training used A I to spot a possible planet, which NASA checks next month.

teaser.who: Amazon, the online retailer, and Meta, with its new Muse A I agent for small businesses; the energy consultancy Wood Mackenzie, relayed by one outlet
teaser.what: Amazon asked Meta last week to remove its store from Muse, an A I agent that can buy and publish for small businesses, saying it had not agreed to be included; Wood Mackenzie found four-hour batteries cheaper than the open-cycle gas turbines many data centre developers favour in all forty-three markets it surveyed

teaser.script: Also in the full report. Amazon wants Meta's shopping helper off its store, hurting small firms. And a study finds batteries cheaper than gas plants for data centres.
